query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The simultaneous resistance to wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) operating in harsh mechanical–corrosive environments is controlled by the alloy’s ability to form and continuously regenerate a protective passive layer. This occurs because a nanocrystalline, chemically homogeneous single-phase structure with sluggish diffusion minimizes local galvanic gradients and fosters rapid repassivation where mechanical damage occurs.
generation.material_initial_state: A uniformly distributed, nanocrystalline HEA that is primarily a single-phase BCC or FCC solid solution with high chemical homogeneity
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to a controlled wear test (e.g., pin-on-disk sliding) in a corrosive medium (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl solution) under conditions that combine mechanical abrasion with corrosive attack
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at room temperature and at an elevated temperature where oxide formation is still favorable, with a defined load and sliding speed to simulate harsh service conditions
generation.structural_mediator: A fine, nanocrystalline grain structure with uniformly distributed elements that reduces local chemical heterogeneity and impedes the formation of detrimental galvanic couples
generation.mechanism: Due to lattice distortions and sluggish atomic diffusion inherent to HEAs, mechanical abrasion creates fresh surfaces that quickly develop a stable, adherent passive oxide layer. This dynamic repassivation minimizes corrosive elemental leaching and maintains high hardness to resist wear. In contrast, alloys with coarser grains or phase segregation would exhibit more pronounced galvanic effects and less effective repassivation, leading to higher degradation rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under combined wear–corrosion conditions, the nanocrystalline HEA should show a lower wear rate and reduced corrosion current density compared to a matched baseline HEA with a coarser or phase-segregated microstructure. Moreover, the oxide/passive layer on the worn surfaces should remain intact and continuous, evidencing rapid regeneration after mechanical disruption.
generation.baseline: A matched HEA of similar chemical composition but with a coarser grain structure or with induced phase segregation that weakens the uniform oxide formation and repassivation
generation.boundary: The prediction is expected to hold in environments that allow the formation of protective oxides (e.g., moderately oxidizing conditions). It may fail in environments that either are too reducing to form a passive layer or in cases where mechanical damage is so severe that the repassivation kinetics cannot keep pace.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contributions of grain size and elemental distribution to the oxide stability and repassivation rate under simultaneous wear and corrosion are not fully established, and the exact threshold beyond which the mechanism fails remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two HEA samples with identical compositions: one processed to achieve a nanocrystalline, homogeneous structure and one intentionally processed to yield a coarser-grained or phase-segregated microstructure. Subject both to pin-on-disk wear testing in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution while monitoring both friction/wear rates and corrosion behavior (e.g., via potentiodynamic polarization). Post-test, use surface analytical techniques such as scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to evaluate the continuity and composition of passive oxide layers across wear tracks.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and continuity (from SEM/XPS)
Surface hardness before and after tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanocrystalline, chemically homogeneous HEA does not exhibit significantly lower wear rates, reduced corrosion current densities, and evidence of rapid passive layer regeneration compared to the coarser baseline alloy, or if no stable passive oxide layer is observed to form on the worn surfaces, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
